title: Great Leaders Cheer
author: The Business Leader Daily
source: The Business Leader Daily on Substack, December 9, 2025
summary: The piece sits in the underrated corner of leadership practice: the direct performance effect of specific, timely encouragement. The frame is that long change initiatives generate periods where progress is real but invisible, and in those stretches the leader's words do more work than the strategy deck. Every sentence and every action becomes part of the emotional climate, and that climate is what determines whether the team shows up the next day with discretionary effort or with the bare minimum. The sharp move is the distinction between recognising results and recognising effort. End-of-project recognition matters, but if it is the only moment the team feels seen, the in-between months teach people that only finished work counts. By naming the late nights, the trade-offs, and the small wins along the way, a leader signals that they understand the difficulty of the journey and care about more than the final deliverable. That combination of empathy and belief is the thing that actually strengthens commitment and fuels the next push. The operating line the author lands on is the one worth carrying into one-to-ones this week: great leaders do not just manage projects, they actively root for their people in a way the people can feel. Encouragement here is not cheerleading or positivity. It is a specific, observable recognition of effort and progress, delivered in-flight rather than at the post-mortem. It is also, the author argues, one of the most underused tools available to a leader trying to hold energy through a slow transformation.
points: The central argument of this piece is grounded in the author's engagement with how real people think and act, not in idealized or abstract reasoning.
The takeaway is actionable,it can be implemented at the classroom or school level without waiting for policy change or external resources.
The piece challenges a common default assumption in education practice and offers a concrete alternative framed by evidence or lived experience.
The stakes are clear: what happens if leaders or teachers adopt this approach, and what is the cost of continuing the current default.
quotes: Navigating complex initiatives and business transformations can feel like an uphill battle. Especially when change initiatives take significant time, and progress moves slowly. How you respond in these moments of pressure significantly influences your team’s morale and performance.

Every word you speak and every action you take echoes throughout the team, shaping their perception of setbacks and opportunities. Your influence goes well beyond task delegation and strategic planning; it determines the emotional climate for how your team shows up each day.
Too many leaders underestimate the impact of timely, genuine encouragement. A few sincere words that recognize effort, learning, or progress can unlock a surge of motivation and discretionary effort.

When you recognize not just the results but also the effort—the late nights, tough trade-offs, and small wins—you’re not just boosting morale. You’re creating a culture where people feel valued and motivated to face the next challenge.
Many leaders fall into the trap of only celebrating when the project is finished. End-of-project recognition matters, but it shouldn’t be the only moment your team feels valued.
By regularly highlighting progress along the way, you send a clear signal: you understand the difficulty of the journey, and you’re invested in more than just the final deliverable.
That combination of empathy and belief reinforces trust, strengthens commitment, and fuels performance. It shows that you care about them as people and that you genuinely want them to succeed.
Great leaders don’t just manage projects; they actively root for their people and make sure their teams can feel it.” Archived from The Business Leader Daily on April 20, 2026 by Tim.
